value.overview: The Cedar Waxwing is a sleek, social songbird named for the red, wax-like tips sometimes found on its wing feathers. It has a smooth brown head and back, a pale yellow belly, a black mask bordered in white, and a yellow-tipped tail. Highly specialized for eating fruit, it often travels in flocks and can swallow berries whole. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon winter visitor rather than a breeding resident.
value.classification: The Cedar Waxwing belongs to the waxwing family, Bombycillidae, and the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Bombycilla cedrorum.
value.identification: This medium-sized waxwing has a prominent crest, short neck, broad pointed wings, and a silky, pale brown to gray-brown body. The face shows a black mask outlined in white, while the throat and upper breast are warm brown. The belly is pale yellow, and the tail ends in a bright yellow band. Adults may show red wax-like feather tips on the wings. Juveniles are duller, streaked, and less sharply marked. Its thin, high-pitched calls are often noticed before the bird is seen.
value.rangeHabitat: The Cedar Waxwing breeds across much of Canada and the northern and central United States, with some resident populations farther south. During the nonbreeding season, it moves through the United States and into Mexico and Central America. In Costa Rica, it is an irregular or sporadic winter visitor, generally reported from December through April and occasionally into mid-May. It is especially associated with elevations of about 500 to 2,000 meters in the central mountains and northern ranges, including fruiting trees, forest edges, gardens, and open wooded habitats.
value.migrationStatus: A short- to medium-distance migrant across most of its range. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly as an uncommon, irregular winter visitor from December to April, with some records extending into May; it does not normally breed there.
value.breeding: Breeding usually takes place from late spring through summer in open woodland, forest edges, parks, and shrubby habitats. Pairs may nest solitarily or near other pairs, often placing a loosely built nest in a tree or large shrub. The female commonly lays about two to six pale, dark-spotted eggs and performs most incubation. Both adults feed the young, and the species may produce one or two broods in a season. Courtship often includes passing berries or other food between partners.
value.dietFeeding: Fruit forms the main part of the diet, especially small berries and fruits from trees and shrubs such as junipers, serviceberries, dogwoods, and mistletoe. Cedar Waxwings also take insects, particularly during the breeding season, when protein is important for nestlings. They frequently forage in flocks, moving through fruiting trees and sometimes catching insects in short aerial sallies. They can pass food directly from one bird to another and may become ill after eating excessive amounts of overripe fruit.
value.behavior: Cedar Waxwings are strongly social and commonly gather in flocks ranging from a few birds to many dozens. They sit conspicuously on exposed branches, communicate with thin, high-pitched calls, and move together between feeding sites. Their flight is direct and undulating. They spend much of the day feeding, preening, and resting near fruiting plants. Outside the breeding period, flock members may remain close together, especially where food is concentrated.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable to increasing overall, although numbers can vary locally and from year to year.
